shows.name: The Curious & Creative Podcast
shows.tagline: Where creative strategy meets real conversation.
shows.about: A deep dive into the minds of artists, creators, and innovators — the ideas, decisions, and cultural moments that shape how we see (and sell) the world.
shows.description: Curiosity and creativity live in constant conversation — and this show lives in that space. Hosted by Janel Moore and Joshua German, Curious & Creative follows the ideas, stories, and cultural moments that have our attention across media, art, society, and everything in between. Some episodes are conversations with guests pushing boundaries in their own lanes. Some are just us unpacking what has our attention. But every episode comes back to the same belief: you don't have to be either curious or creative. You're both... and then some.

shows.name: The Eclectic Polymath Podcast
shows.tagline: Everything is interesting when you dig deep enough.
shows.about: Deep, well-researched episodes on whatever's too interesting to ignore: history and power, religion and myth, psychology, science, and Black culture. No lane, no niche.
shows.feed_title: The Eclectic Polymath with Joshua German
shows.description:
There’s too much interesting stuff in the world to only care about one thing.
The Eclectic Polymath Podcast explores a different curiosity every episode: fascinating people, strange moments in history, cultural shifts, political movements, religions, technologies, music, myths, ideas, and questions you may never have thought to ask.
Some episodes explain how something became the way it is. Others unpack the life of someone worth knowing, trace an idea across centuries, or follow one rabbit hole until it connects to five others.
You don’t need to be an expert. You just need to stay curious.

shows.name: Approachable AI
shows.tagline: Demystifying AI, one episode at a time.
shows.about: No jargon, just what's actually happening and why it matters. Real tools, real builds, and the mistakes along the way.
shows.description: Welcome to Approachable AI: Your shortcut to understanding artificial intelligence in plain English. We explore what’s happening, why it matters, and how you can use it so that AI feels less like the future and more like a part of your everyday routine.

shows.name: Too Much to Tweet
shows.tagline: The takes too big for a caption.
shows.about: Politics, culture, and the conversations the internet keeps trying to flatten into a thread.

shows.name: Dominate the Decade
shows.tagline: Growth, culture, and building a meaningful decade.
shows.about: Three young Black men navigating their own paths to success — crypto, politics, sports, music, movies, and everything in between. The full 2020–2023 run, including Janel's guest episode.
shows.description: Three black young men, each navigating their individual paths to success. Follow along and join in as we strive to dominate the decade in all aspects of life.

shows.description: Welcome to Aspiring Abolitionist, the podcast where we dive into the political, social, and cultural moments shaping our world today.

shows.name: The Jazz Riff
shows.tagline: Jazz only, four times a week.
shows.description: The Riff is a jazz briefing from Curious & Creative. New episodes four times a week — Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays. The news, the new albums, the history, and what's actually happening in the Los Angeles jazz scene this week — from the big rooms to the tiny ones you only hear about on Instagram. Up First, but for jazz: tight, inside, and straight to the music. Love you madly.

shows.name: God is Brazilian
shows.description:
God is Brazilian — and once you understand the country, you'll know why they say it.
Deep dives into the biggest, loudest, most contradictory country in the Americas: its epic history, its megacities (São Paulo, Rio, Salvador), its music — samba, pagode, bossa nova, and the artists who defied a dictatorship — its money (Pix and the fintech revolution), its scandals, its Black resistance, and its rise as a 21st-century global power.
Every topic arrives as a pair: one episode in English, one in Português, released together.
Hosted by Joshua German. Part of the Curious & Creative network.

shows.name: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
shows.short: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
shows.feed_title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
shows.description: Once Upon a Time in Harlem is a deep-dive documentary podcast about the Harlem Renaissance — one person, one place, or one thing at a time. The poets and pianists, yes, but also the librarian who introduced them to each other, the numbers banker who paid for the prizes, the salon where the arguments happened, and the ballroom where the dance was invented. Inspired by William and David Greaves' film of the same name. A Curious & Creative production.

episodes.title: #253 The Missing Pact: Why Asia Never Built Its NATO
episodes.description:
Europe came out of the Second World War and built a table: NATO, pooled coal and steel, eventually a shared history textbook between France and Germany. East Asia came out of the same war and built a wheel. The United States sits at the hub, and Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, and Taiwan each hold a separate spoke, facing Washington one at a time and rarely each other. This episode asks why. The answer is not that Asia's nations failed to organize. It is that the system was designed, in San Francisco in 1951, so they would not have to, and so Washington would never lose control of clients it feared might drag it into a larger war.
 We trace the founding bargain that kept Emperor…

episodes.title: #252 Godzilla: The Monster Japan Built to Carry Its Grief
episodes.description:
On November 3, 1954, Japanese audiences filed into theaters to watch a monster destroy Tokyo. Gojira was not escapism. It arrived nine years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, two years after an Allied occupation that had forbidden the country to speak publicly about the atomic bombings, and eight months after an American hydrogen bomb test irradiated the crew of the fishing boat Lucky Dragon No. 5. This episode tells the story of what Godzilla actually is: not a movie monster later read as a metaphor, but a nation's grief given a body.
 We trace the years of silence under occupation censorship, the hibakusha literature and testimony that carried the witness the films could not, and the…

episodes.title: #251 Arnold Schwarzenegger: The Recall That Invented the Celebrity Candidate
episodes.description:
In October 2003, California fired its governor mid-term — and replaced him with a movie star. This episode traces how the 2003 gubernatorial recall worked, who paid for it, why Gray Davis was so unpopular, and how Arnold Schwarzenegger turned stardom into campaign infrastructure — from the 135-candidate ballot to the Year of Reform, the governing arc from 65 percent approval to 37 and back, and the legacy the recall normalized: celebrity as a path to power.

episodes.description:

episodes.title: The Sweep: Six Cities, Halloween Week
episodes.description:
The Sweep is back — six cities, one week, and the week ends on Halloween. New York opens with Mike LeDonne's 70th-birthday big band at Jazz at Lincoln Center and closes with Robert Glasper's Halloween run at the Blue Note; Chicago answers with ten-dollar Green Mill Mondays and a Coltrane tribute at the Jazz Showcase.
 London runs through Ronnie Scott's with Joel Ross and Sullivan Fortner, Paris answers with James Brandon Lewis and Mark Guiliana at the New Morning, and Tokyo turns the whole Asagaya neighborhood into a bandstand for Jazz Streets. At home in LA: KATALYST's Halloween Vibes at Blue Note Los Angeles is the week's pick.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #21 Lula and the ABC Metalworkers: How a Factory Worker Built a Political Movement (English)
episodes.description:
In 1978, in the factory towns outside São Paulo, thousands of autoworkers found a protest the dictatorship could not shoot: they walked into the plant, stood at their machines, and crossed their arms. Arms crossed, machines stopped. The man leading them was a 32-year-old lathe operator who had left school as a child, migrated 3,000 kilometres from Pernambuco in the back of a truck, and lost a finger in a factory press.
 This episode tells how that moment became a movement. The wage squeeze and the falsified inflation numbers that gave the ABC metalworkers an arithmetic grievance, the stadium assemblies at Vila Euclides where tens of thousands learned their own size, the church doors that…

episodes.title: Monday, October 26, 2026
episodes.description:
Lula da Silva wins a historic fourth term in Brazil as Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede and vows to seek annulment. Plus: Serbia's student movement topples Vučić; France's second protest Saturday and the November 5 strike call; Houthi attacks empty Saudi skies; the midterms in a Sunday courtroom; Israel on election eve; the Fed and big-tech week; and Ebola responders attacked in Congo.
 Stories: Brazil's runoff · Serbia's student victory · France · Saudi Arabia and the Houthis · The midterms and the courts · Israel's election · Markets and the AI ledger · Congo and Ebola.
 Part of the Curious & Creative network. Back tomorrow morning.

episodes.title: #239 The Greenville Clowns: The Monster Nobody Ever Found
episodes.description:
In late August 2016, a mother in Greenville, South Carolina reported what her son had seen in the woods behind their apartment complex: clowns, whispering, flashing green lights, trying to lure children in. Deputies searched the abandoned house by the pond and found nothing. Within nine days the story was national. Within six weeks it was a worldwide panic — school lockdowns, clown hunts, a benched Ronald McDonald, a question at a White House briefing.
 This episode reconstructs the whole cascade from the Greenville file itself, which is the strangest document in the story: no clown was ever found, photographed credibly, or arrested there, and there was never a case. It also traces the…

episodes.title: #238 Jay-Z vs. Nas: Two Casinos, Two Theories of Black Capital
episodes.description:
In September 2025, New York ran the same experiment twice. Jay-Z stood before a community committee and pitched a Caesars casino in the middle of Times Square: "We from these neighborhoods. We are the community." The committee voted him down, 4 to 2. Eight days later, Queens voted 6 to 0 for a $5.5 billion Resorts World expansion with Nas as its hometown face — and the borough president cast his yes while quoting "Queens Get the Money."
 This episode reconstructs both fights: the Broadway coalition that killed the Times Square bid, the governor, mayor, and building trades who backed it anyway, and the consent-first Queens campaign that never faced a single speaker against it. It keeps the…

episodes.title: #5 Richard Bruce Nugent: The Rebel Who Outlived the Harlem Renaissance
episodes.description:
In November 1926, a twenty-year-old who signed himself "Richard Bruce" published "Smoke, Lilies and Jade" in the single issue of Fire!! — the first published literary work by an African American to write openly about homosexuality. It ended with the words "To Be Continued." The continuation never came. Almost everything about Richard Bruce Nugent arrived late — including the recognition.
 This episode follows him through the young Harlem that made him: the Fire!! editorial board alongside Thurman, Hughes, and Hurston; the rooming house at 267 West 136th Street — "Niggerati Manor" — whose walls he covered with murals; the magazine that burned in an actual fire while Thurman paid off its…

episodes.title: #237 Obama's Incomplete Bill: The Healthcare Law That Never Finished the Job
episodes.description:
When Barack Obama signed the Affordable Care Act in March 2010, he called it the culmination of a century’s fight. Fifteen years later, even its defenders reach for the same word: incomplete. This episode takes that word apart — because the bill was left unfinished in three different ways, and they are not the same story.
 Part of it was designed out: the public option traded away senator by senator, the deals cut with the drug and hospital industries, a law built on private insurers from the first sketch. Part of it was cut out: the Supreme Court made Medicaid expansion optional, opening a coverage gap that today holds about 1.2 million people, disproportionately Black and Southern. And…

episodes.title: #4 Casper Holstein: The Numbers Banker Who Bankrolled the Renaissance
episodes.description:
In 1920s Harlem, the biggest bank in the neighborhood wasn't a bank. It was an illegal lottery run by Casper Holstein — a St. Croix-born former Wall Street messenger who built his numbers game, Bolito, on the New York Clearing House's own published figures: a daily winning number that nobody could fix.
 About half of Harlem played on any given day. The game turned over tens of millions of dollars a year and employed roughly a thousand collectors — and Holstein poured the profit back into the community. In 1926 he put up the $1,000 that endowed Opportunity magazine's literary prizes, the Casper Holstein Awards, and historian David Levering Lewis counted him among the six most important…

episodes.title: The Week Ahead: October 26 – November 1
episodes.description:
The Week Ahead, October 26 – November 1: the full rundown — news, new wax, and what's actually happening in Los Angeles, from the big rooms to the tiny ones. Christian McBride hands the keys to his young band Ursa Major on Points of Light, produced by Terrace Martin and out Friday on Mack Avenue, and the Miles/Coltrane Legacy tour carries the twin centennials of 2026.
 In LA: Jason Moran plays Duke Ellington with the Pacific Symphony at Segerstrom Hall, John Scofield's Electrospective at the Regent, Stanley Clarke in Glendale, and the week's pick — the Covell album-release night at Sam First with Joe La Barbera and Mark Turner. From the vault: Clifford Brown, born October 30, 1930.
 Love…

episodes.title: #3 A'Lelia Walker and the Dark Tower: The Salon That Ran Harlem
episodes.description:
When Madam C.J. Walker died in 1919, her daughter A'Lelia inherited a fortune, two Harlem townhouses, and a question nobody could answer for her: what is Black wealth supposed to DO? Her answer was the Dark Tower — a salon on 136th Street, named for a Countee Cullen poem, decorated like a skyscraper, where poets and painters mixed with numbers bankers and downtown millionaires.
 Langston Hughes called her the joy goddess of Harlem's 1920s. Her great-granddaughter's biography calls her something more deliberate: an institution builder who co-designed the salon with the artists it served, asking them, "What is it that you would like?"
 This episode follows the money, the guest lists, the…

episodes.title: #3 A'Lelia Walker and the Dark Tower: The Salon That Ran Harlem
episodes.description:
When Madam C.J. Walker died in 1919, her daughter A'Lelia inherited a fortune, two Harlem townhouses, and a question nobody could answer for her: what is Black wealth supposed to DO? Her answer was the Dark Tower — a salon on 136th Street, named for a Countee Cullen poem, decorated like a skyscraper, where poets and painters mixed with numbers bankers and downtown millionaires.
 Langston Hughes called her the joy goddess of Harlem's 1920s. Her great-granddaughter's biography calls her something more deliberate: an institution builder who co-designed the salon with the artists it served, asking them, "What is it that you would like?"
 This episode follows the money, the guest lists, the…

episodes.title: #2 Regina Anderson Andrews: The Librarian Who Wired the Renaissance
episodes.description:
At her NYPL interview, Regina Anderson wrote "American" in the race box. The administrator told her: to us, you're not. She was routed to the one branch Black librarians were confined to — the 135th Street branch in Harlem — and proceeded to turn it into the Harlem Renaissance's switchboard.
 From that desk she programmed the lectures and exhibitions, hosted the writers at her apartment up the avenue, and helped plan the 1924 Civic Club dinner that launched a generation. Langston Hughes met Arna Bontemps in her rooms. Aaron Douglas got his landing place there. She also wrote plays of her own, fought forty years for every promotion grade, and was still there in 1972, on camera at the Greaves…

episodes.title: #236 Harold Washington: The Mayor Who Beat the Machine
episodes.description:
Harold Washington didn't inherit Chicago. He registered it. Before the 1983 run he set a condition: 50,000 new Black voters, or no campaign. Black Chicago delivered nearly double, and the machine that had run the city for half a century met the one candidate it couldn't absorb.
 This episode goes deep on the whole arc: the Daley machine and the Black submachine Washington came up under, the ugliest general election in modern Chicago history, and the Council Wars that froze his first term. Then the record itself: the appointments, Executive Order 85-2 opening city contracts, Fair Share budgeting, and what it concretely meant for Black Chicago.
 And finally the two legacies: "Harold," the…

episodes.title: #1 The Party: The Night the Renaissance Came Back to One Room
episodes.description:
In August 1972, filmmaker William Greaves threw a cocktail party at Duke Ellington's Harlem townhouse and invited every surviving creator of the Harlem Renaissance he could find. Three cameras rolled for hours. Then the footage sat unfinished for 54 years.
 This founding episode tells the whole story: who Greaves was, what happened in that room (the arguments, the poetry, 96-year-old Leigh Whipper reciting from memory, James Van Der Zee sitting down at Ellington's piano), why the film took three generations of one family to finish, and how it finally premiered in 2026 to a Library of Congress prize.
 Then we walk the room. All 26 guests get their introduction here — because every one of…

episodes.title: #20 Como os Brasileiros Realmente Trabalham: Salários, Direitos e o Dia a Dia (Português)
episodes.description:
No Brasil, uma pergunta discreta decide toda a sua vida de trabalho: a sua carteira é assinada? Carteira assinada significa décimo terceiro, 30 dias de férias pagas mais um terço, fundo de garantia, aposentadoria e uma Justiça do Trabalho atrás de você. Sem assinatura, você é um dos cerca de 40 milhões de brasileiros informais construindo a vida sem nada desse chão.
 Este episódio caminha pelos dois lados dessa linha. De Vargas e da CLT de 1943, que ergueu a catedral formal, aos custos do empregador que empurraram milhões para fora dela, à ponte do MEI que virou brecha, às trabalhadoras domésticas que esperaram até 2013 por direitos na mesa da cozinha, e aos entregadores de aplicativo em…

episodes.title: #20 How Brazilians Actually Work: Wages, Labor Rights and Everyday Life (English)
episodes.description:
In Brazil, one question quietly decides your whole working life: is your card signed? A signed carteira means a 13th salary, 30 days of paid vacation plus a third, a severance fund, a pension, and a labor court behind you. No signature, and you are one of roughly 40 million informal Brazilians building a living without any of that floor.
 This episode walks both sides of that line. From Vargas and the 1943 CLT that built the formal cathedral, to the employer costs that pushed millions outside it, the MEI bridge that became a loophole, the domestic workers who waited until 2013 for rights at the kitchen table, and the app riders striking for R$10 a delivery. Plus meal vouchers as a second…

episodes.title: #235 Ryū Murakami: The Other Murakami
episodes.description:
On October 23, 2026, Japan learned that Ryū Murakami was dead, and almost every English-language obituary had to begin the same way: not that Murakami. This episode is about the one the world mostly didn't read: the novelist who grew up in the shadow of an American naval base, won Japan's biggest literary prize at 24 with a novel of drugs and drift, and spent fifty years writing the people postwar Japan's success story left behind.
 Inside: Coin Locker Babies and the masterpiece that took fifteen years to reach English; the double-Murakami rivalry, including the sense of competition Haruki himself says helped push him to become a novelist; Audition, Miike, and the Western cult that credited…

episodes.title: The Sweep: The Week of the Big Band
episodes.description:
The Sweep is back: six cities, one week, and this time the big bands are carrying it. A fourteen-piece Mingus band holds Ronnie Scott's all week, the Count Basie Orchestra sets up in Tokyo, and Chicago answers with an octet and Dee Alexander, while two festivals play their final nights.
 Robert Glasper's Robtober hits its closing stretch at Blue Note New York (Questlove and Bilal on Wednesday, Wyclef Jean Thursday and Friday, Kem on the weekend), Joshua Redman opens three nights at Blue Note Tokyo, Marquis Hill sells out the Duc des Lombards in Paris, and Los Angeles closes the Angel City Jazz Festival in the small rooms where it lives.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #234 The Spice Wars: The Seed That Outpriced Manhattan
episodes.description:
In 1667, England and the Netherlands signed a peace that left the Dutch holding Run, a nutmeg island three kilometres long, and the English holding a muddy port called Manhattan. By the prices of the day, the Dutch won. This episode tells the story of how that could possibly be true: three thousand years of wars fought over flavor.
 It starts with salt, the spice nobody calls a spice: China's two-thousand-year state monopoly and the smugglers who nearly toppled dynasties, Sahara caravans trading salt almost weight for weight with gold, France's gabelle and the three thousand people a year punished for salt, and Gandhi's handful of shore salt against an empire. Then pepper, the black gold…

episodes.title: #233 McDonald's Monopoly: Why You're Always One Piece Away
episodes.description:
You have never won McDonald's Monopoly, and neither has anyone you know — but you have absolutely been one piece away. This episode opens the machine up: who invented the promotion in 1987, how the odds are actually printed, why the law requires a mail-in route that gives you the same chance for the price of two stamps, and the twelve years when the winning pieces were being stolen from the inside.
 Inside: the rare-piece design (in the 2014 rules, Boardwalk was a single piece at 1 in 651,841,628); the psychology of the near-miss; Jerome Jacobson, the security chief who ran the theft ring until the FBI's Operation Final Answer took down 51 people in August 2001 — weeks before 9/11 buried…

episodes.title: #232 Epstein's Last Men Standing: The Lawyer and Accountant Nobody Charged
episodes.description:
For two decades, Jeffrey Epstein's operation ran through two professionals: his lawyer Darren Indyke and his accountant Richard Kahn. On October 21, 2026, New Mexico's attorney general sued them — the first law-enforcement action either man has ever faced. This episode asks who they are, what the documented record actually shows, and why accountability arrived as a civil suit seven years after Epstein's death.
 Inside: the 1953 Trust in Epstein's own words (the $50 million and $25 million bequests, the forgiven debts); the estate's full arithmetic, from $577 million to the $121 million paid to 136 claimants; their sworn congressional denials; the banks that paid hundreds of millions while…

episodes.title: #231 Eisenkot: The General Running to Replace Netanyahu
episodes.description:
Five days before Israel votes, the man leading half the polls is a general who has never held office — and the math says nobody can win. This episode reconstructs Gadi Eisenkot's rise, the party he built in a year, and the deadlock waiting on the other side of October 27.
 Inside: the son he buried and the doctrine he wrote; Gantz's exit and the threshold arithmetic behind it; the red line he read into the record ("I will not serve under Netanyahu"); the state-inquiry fight driving the whole election; and the honest counter-case — the ten-poll average actually has Likud ahead, and Israel's generals have a mixed record once they take the chair.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay…

episodes.title: Thursday, October 22, 2026
episodes.description:
The United States orders its diplomats out of Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks close in on the kingdom, with US and Israel strike plans on Iran flagged as developing. Plus: France bans the next protest wave, Zelensky floats a freeze formula, Brazil's runoff stays a coin flip four days out, and a Budapest dachshund closes the show.
 Stories: Saudi Arabia and the Houthis · Iran strike plans (developing) · France's protest bans · Ukraine's freeze formula · The midterms · Brazil's runoff · Markets and Meta · The UNEP emissions gap · The Buda dachshund.
 Part of the Curious & Creative network. Back tomorrow morning.

episodes.title: #230 Lovecraft Country: The Hit HBO Cancelled and Never Explained
episodes.description: A hit show, cancelled after one season, by a network that never explained why. Lovecraft Country grew its audience all season, topped HBO Max, and pulled 18 Emmy nominations, including Drama Series, eleven days after HBO ended it. A second season, Supremacy, existed on paper, complete with a map of a divided America built on the finale's spell. So what actually happened? This episode reconstructs the decision from the record: the numbers by their separate measures, the cost nobody ever sourced, the graded causes (economics, a book that ended, an institution mid-merger, and one anonymously sourced account that must be carried carefully), and Casey Bloys' only explanation: "a confluence of…

episodes.title: #229 Jonathan Majors: The Villain Who Broke Marvel's Timeline
episodes.description:
He was supposed to be everywhere. Marvel built its Multiverse Saga on one actor playing infinite variants of the same villain — then a Manhattan jury, a split verdict, and a firing within hours ended it. This episode reconstructs the whole braid: Jonathan Majors' trial count by count, the Kang architecture across Loki and Quantumania, the timeline that was designed and the one that actually happened, and how Marvel replaced a saga with a mask it already owned.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #228 Are Redheads Black? The Gene, the Pharaoh, and the Meme
episodes.description:
In May 2025, the internet declared redheads Black — and meant it at least five different ways. This episode separates the claims and tests each one: the genetics of the red-hair gene and where its mutations actually arose, a redheaded pharaoh under a Paris microscope, Malcolm X's family tree, and the Melanesian islanders who evolved red hair through a completely different gene. What's literally true, what's a distortion, and what's false — layer by layer.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #227 Asteroid Mining: Humanity's Next Industry
episodes.description:
What is actually out there, and what could it mean for us if we could reach it? Asteroids are failed planets, frozen feedstock from the solar system's construction, and water locked in clay older than Earth. This episode explores what asteroid mining really is: the metal cores of shattered worlds, the platinum-group metals the hydrogen economy is running short on, and the gas stations floating at the top of Earth's gravity well.
 Along the way: the missions that already went out and touched them (Hayabusa2, OSIRIS-REx, NASA's Psyche, China's Tianwen-2), the startups that tried and died, how close the technology honestly is, the price paradox that breaks the famous business model, who owns…

episodes.title: #226 The Envelope: How Moonlight Really Won.
episodes.description:
It is still the most shocking moment in Oscars history: La La Land announced as Best Picture, speeches underway — then the correction. Moonlight had won. This episode reconstructs that night minute by minute and asks the question underneath it: the count was never wrong, only the envelope was. So what actually failed?
 Inside: the duplicate card that survived in the wrong set, the backstage photo tweeted minutes before the handoff, how preferential voting really works, why the results are memorized and written down nowhere, PwC's role since 1935 and the sealed envelope born in 1941, and the counterfactual the system cannot answer — if the count itself were ever wrong, no one would ever…

episodes.title: Wednesday, October 21, 2026
episodes.description:
France's protest wave reaches the town halls, with the Limoges city hall burned overnight and fresh nationwide protests called for Saturday. Plus: Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, flagged as developing; Brazil four days from a runoff that's still a statistical tie; Israel's first polls since Gantz walked; the Congo wire under White House inquiry; Trump's $400 million midterm commitment; Banijay's CEO tells the streamers to give producers their IP back; and Japan launches a spacecraft to a Martian moon.
 Stories: France and the town halls · Saudi Arabia and Yemen · Brazil's runoff · Israel's polls · The Congo wire (developing) · The midterms · The business of entertainment · Japan's Phobos…

episodes.title: #225 Mike & Pam: The Last Studio Heads of Hollywood
episodes.description:
Six consecutive number-one openings. A Best Picture winner. The best studio year of the decade. It still wasn't enough. When the Paramount Skydance merger closed in October 2026, Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy were out at Warner Bros. This episode is their complete arc, and what it says about who gets to run Hollywood now.
 Inside: the lineage (a German-Jewish immigrant mother and an Italian-American father in Brooklyn; a Syrian American father and an Italian American family in Florham Park with a mob history the profiles skip), the bottom-rung starts (his story department desk at New Line at twenty, her receptionist chair at Danny DeVito's company), the reigns at New Line and New Regency, the…

episodes.title: #004 The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
episodes.description:
Fresh out of the theater, Joshua and Janel share their thoughts on The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . They get into the film, its cast, and the role New York plays in the story.
 Stay curious. Stay creative.

episodes.title: #19 A "Democracia Racial" do Brasil: Mito, Realidade e o Significado de Raça (Português)
episodes.description:
#19 A "Democracia Racial" do Brasil: Mito, Realidade e o Significado de Raça (Português)
 O Brasil contou ao mundo uma história bonita sobre si mesmo: nada de Jim Crow, nada de linha de cor, um país tão mestiço que o racismo nunca teve chance. Por décadas, boa parte do mundo acreditou. O Brasil também acreditou.
 Este episódio desmonta essa história. De Casa-Grande & Senzala, de Gilberto Freyre, em 1933, e a celebração da mestiçagem, aos pesquisadores da UNESCO que chegaram nos anos 1950 esperando uma sociedade modelo e documentaram preconceito, até Florestan Fernandes e sua frase devastadora, o "preconceito de não ter preconceito". E ainda Abdias do Nascimento e o movimento negro que…

episodes.title: #19 Brazil's "Racial Democracy": Myth, Reality and the Meaning of Race (English)
episodes.description:
#19 Brazil's "Racial Democracy": Myth, Reality and the Meaning of Race (English)
 Brazil told the world a beautiful story about itself: no Jim Crow, no color line, a country so mixed that racism never stood a chance. For decades, a lot of the world believed it. Brazil believed it too.
 This episode takes that story apart. From Gilberto Freyre's Casa-Grande & Senzala in 1933 and the celebration of mestiçagem, to the UNESCO researchers who arrived in the 1950s expecting a model society and documented prejudice instead, to Florestan Fernandes and his devastating phrase, the "prejudice of having no prejudice." Plus Abdias do Nascimento and the Black movement that named the myth in public, and…

episodes.title: #18 A Franquia Bolsonaro: A Família que Virou um Movimento (Português)
episodes.description:
#18 A Franquia Bolsonaro: A Família que Virou um Movimento (Português)
 Em 4 de outubro de 2026, o Brasil votou — e o maior vencedor não estava na cédula. Jair Bolsonaro está condenado, inelegível até 2030 e proibido de usar redes sociais. O movimento dele acaba de ter a melhor noite da sua história. O filho mais velho, Flávio, venceu o primeiro turno contra o presidente Lula, e os dois se enfrentam de novo no segundo turno, em 25 de outubro.
 Então como um movimento sobrevive ao silenciamento do seu fundador? Este episódio entra na empresa familiar: como Flávio virou o herdeiro, o irmão que toca a política externa a partir do exílio no Texas, a madrasta que talvez seja a política mais…

episodes.title: #18 The Bolsonaro Franchise: The Family That Became a Movement (English)
episodes.description:
#18 The Bolsonaro Franchise: The Family That Became a Movement (English)
 On October 4, 2026, Brazil voted — and the biggest winner was not on the ballot. Jair Bolsonaro is convicted, barred from office until 2030, and banned from social media. His movement just had its best night ever. His eldest son Flávio won the first round against President Lula, and the two meet again in a runoff on October 25.
 So how does a movement outlive the silencing of its founder? This episode goes inside the family firm: how Flávio became the heir, the brother running foreign policy from exile in Texas, the stepmother who may be the family's most popular politician, and the party machine underneath them all —…

episodes.title: #224 Flávio Bolsonaro: The Heir, the Exile, and the Algorithm
episodes.description:
On October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of Brazil's presidential election, 56.1 million votes to 53.9 million. His father, the man who built the movement, followed it under house arrest: 27 years for the coup plot, barred from office until 2030, banned from even posting online.
 So how is the movement winning? This episode maps the succession: the heir chosen from custody, the brother running foreign policy from exile in Texas, the stepmother and brothers winning Senate seats of their own, the biggest party in Congress, a billion reais a year in public money, and a runoff being fought inside Instagram's algorithm, with Brazil's electoral court fining Meta into…

episodes.title: #223 The Yellow Jackets: France's Permanent Revolt
episodes.description:
Every car in France carried the uniform. The law put it there. In November 2018 the drivers of the periphery put it on, seized the roundabouts, and cancelled a fuel tax in eighteen days.
 No leaders. No party. Nobody who could sign a peace. So how did a movement that could not negotiate win some €10 billion, freeze France's carbon tax for eight years and counting, and still elect nobody? The dress rehearsals in red caps. The parliament of traffic circles. The eye injuries and the €135 vest. And why the vests came back out of the trunk in October 2026, this time marching behind students.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #222 What's going on in France?… and why?
episodes.description:
Half a million people in the streets. Schoolkids sitting on top of the Republic's own statue. Town halls burning by night. And no leader anywhere who can call it off, because nobody called it on.
 This started with a school in Créteil that had no teachers. It became the biggest test yet of how France actually governs itself: through the street. Why French governments retreat, when they don't, and why a movement nobody leads might be the hardest kind to beat, and the easiest kind to outlast. Plus what it sets up for 2027, when Macron is gone and Le Pen is waiting.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #221 The Homestead: Who Got Set Up, Who Got Stripped
episodes.description:
The United States once ran the largest wealth-building program in its history: 160 acres, nearly free, to anyone who would work it. About a quarter of American adults today descend from the people who got it.
 This is the compare and contrast. What a setup looks like when it comes with a deed, protected title, credit, and institutions behind it, and what it looks like when it doesn't: freedpeople handed 400,000 acres and then stripped of them within the year, Black farmers who built to 15 million acres by 1910 and lost most of it, and the Native nations whose land the free land was. Then the sequel: the same play run again through FHA mortgages and Levittown, where uniformity itself became…

episodes.title: #003: Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother
episodes.description:
What happens when faith, family, and survival collide? Janel and Joshua unpack Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother , a Mahershala Ali-led thriller that blends action, religion, and the complicated realities of parenthood.
 From Black Muslim representation and religious hypocrisy to motherhood, grief, and the sacrifices we make for family, the conversation takes plenty of unexpected turns, including a deep dive into Mormon missionaries.
 Follow Curious & Creative as we explore where culture, curiosity, and creativity meet. 
 Stay curious. Stay creative.

episodes.title: #220 Nathan Fielder: The Man Who Rehearsed Reality
episodes.description:
He has a business degree, a pilot’s license, and a theory about why people don’t speak up.
 Nathan Fielder turned a small-business advice show into a series of experiments on how people comply, perform, and go along: a coffee shop that ran on parody law, a jacket company built on a joke that stopped being one, and a finale that quietly became the best film of its year. Then The Rehearsal scaled the method up, simulations inside simulations, until a season of television about cockpit communication ended with him at the controls of a real 737 full of actors, arguing with the FAA on CNN. This episode is about the lens itself: how the deadpan, the paperwork, and the escalating commitment…

episodes.title: #219 The Grove & The Americana: Fake Towns, Real Empire
episodes.description:
Rick Caruso's father swept floors at the Farmers Market. The son built a town next door.
 The Grove opened in 2002 after fifteen years of failed schemes and neighborhood war, and then out-sold almost every real mall in America. The Americana opened in Glendale in 2008, backed by a redevelopment agency, fought by the mall across the street all the way to a jury, and walked straight into the financial crisis. Both are still standing. This is the story of the trolley, the fountain, the percentage rents nobody else dared charge, the rival who ended up bankrupt while Caruso bought his anchor store out from under him, and the building philosophy that embarrassed every public megaproject in Los…

episodes.title: #218 Nicole Avant: Power, Marriage, and the Family Way
episodes.description:
Nicole Avant grew up in the most connected house in Black Hollywood, and then she built a bigger one.
 Ambassador to the Bahamas at 41. The producer who willed The Black Godfather into existence. Half of the couple whose Hancock Park home runs Democratic politics like an embassy. But the real story is the family playbook: Clarence Avant built the deals, Jacqueline Avant built the culture and the institutions, and Nicole joined what she inherited to the biggest platform in entertainment. What actually gets built when powerful families merge, and why the people at the top keep choosing exactly that. With a nod to #184, our Mellody Hobson episode, and the other half of the pattern.
 Follow…

episodes.title: #217 A Different World: The Sitcom That Refused to End
episodes.description:
A Different World is not a nostalgia story anymore. The Netflix sequel premiered September 24, hit number one in the US, and got renewed eight days later, with Debbie Allen still holding the wheel nearly 40 years after she first saved the show.
 You remember Whitley and Dwayne, the flip-up glasses, and Thursday nights behind The Cosby Show, when Hillman finished as high as number 2 in all of television and number 1 in Black households. What most people missed: season one was a flop with critics, Lisa Bonet was gone within a year, and the show only became itself when a Howard alumna took over and started sending her writers to real Black colleges.
 This episode covers the Allen…

episodes.title: #216 How Karen Bass Became the Establishment
episodes.description:
The police union spent against Karen Bass in 2022. This year it is spending millions for her. That flip tells you most of what you need to know about the mayor Los Angeles is deciding whether to keep.
 You may know her as the first Black woman to lead a state legislature in American history, the congresswoman behind the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, or the mayor who declared a homelessness emergency on day one. Before all of it, she was a physician assistant in the county emergency room during the crack epidemic, watching the same families come back night after night.
 This episode follows the organizer who built Community Coalition out of that emergency room, the reformer whose…

episodes.title: #215 Nithya Raman: Hollywood's Socialist Is Leading the Mayor's Race
episodes.description:
Nineteen days before the election, the challenger is ahead. Nithya Raman endorsed Mayor Karen Bass for re-election in January, then filed to run against her hours before the February deadline, and the September Berkeley IGS poll has her leading the incumbent 39 to 28.
 You may know her as the "Hollywood socialist" from Council District 4, or from the rent cap fight that rewrote the rules for some 650,000 rent-stabilized homes. Before any of that, she was a six-year-old immigrant from Kerala, an urban planner mapping slums in Delhi and Chennai, and the city staffer who found that nearly 90% of LA's homelessness spending went to jailing people.
 This episode traces how that planner became the…

episodes.title: #21 The Week Ahead: October 19-25
episodes.description:
The Week Ahead, October 19–25: the full rundown — news, new wax, and what's actually happening in Los Angeles, from the big rooms to the tiny ones. Samara Joy's Boston Pops announcement, a Verve live album on the way, and Immanuel Wilkins's MacArthur Fellowship lead the news.
 In LA: Talib Kweli and Rapsody at Blue Note LA, Christian Sands at Sam First, Denise Donatelli at Catalina, Angel City's Jazz Refractions weekend (October 23–24), and Sunday Jazz at the World Stage in Leimert Park on October 25. From the vault: Jimmy Heath, born October 25, 1926 — his centennial.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #20 Lakecia Benjamin: Alto Fire
episodes.description:
Lakecia Benjamin broke her jaw in a September 2021 car crash, taught herself to play again with her mouth barely open, and came back with Phoenix — the defining record of her career. A Washington Heights kid who did the sideman years with Stevie Wonder, Alicia Keys, and the Roots is now the bandstand everybody else has to meet.
 Pursuance reimagined the Coltranes, Phoenix turned survival into sound, and the new album We Dream arrived this summer. Listening picks: Pursuance: The Coltranes (2020) and Phoenix (2023).
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #19 Sun Ra: The Man from Saturn
episodes.description:
He said he was from Saturn, changed his name in 1952, ran his Arkestra like a monastery in a Philadelphia rowhouse at 5626 Morton Street, and pressed his own records on El Saturn because no label moved at his speed. Sun Ra did not wait for permission from this planet.
 Space Is the Place on record (1973) and film (1974), the Arkestra still playing under Marshall Allen today, and Lights on a Satellite in 2024. Listening picks: Jazz in Silhouette, The Futuristic Sounds of Sun Ra, and Lanquidity.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #18 Jazz Is Dead: Adrian Younge's Time Machine
episodes.description:
Adrian Younge and Ali Shaheed Muhammad do not sample the legends — they bring them into Linear Labs in Highland Park, record all-analog to tape on vintage gear, and make new albums with them as co-composers. Jazz Is Dead is a time machine that only travels forward.
 The catalog runs JID001 to JID027 — start with Jazz Is Dead 001, then Roy Ayers JID002 and Lonnie Liston Smith JID017 — plus The Midnight Hour, and the Lodge Room live shows running since December 2017.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #17 Tokyo: The City That Listens Hardest
episodes.description:
Every jazz city has a sound; Tokyo has a way of hearing. The city built whole rooms around listening — jazz kissa where the owner played a full side loud and you kept quiet — turned scarce imported records into an education, and pressed vinyl so carefully collectors pay extra for the paper band around the sleeve.
 Chigusa in Yokohama (1933), Blue Note Tokyo (1988), Tower Records Japan outliving its American parent, and players from Sadao Watanabe and Toshiko Akiyoshi to Hiromi. Listening picks: Tsuyoshi Yamamoto's Midnight Sugar and Isao Suzuki's Blow Up.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #16 Kamasi Washington: The Orchestrator
episodes.description:
Kamasi Washington thinks in orchestras. In spring 2015 he wrote string arrangements for Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly, then released The Epic — three discs, a ten-piece band, a 32-piece orchestra, a twenty-person choir — and re-scaled what a jazz album can be.
 Inglewood, Leimert Park, the West Coast Get Down, then Heaven and Earth and Fearless Movement. Listening pick: "Change of the Guard," the opener of The Epic.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #15 Stones Throw at 30: Jazz in Hip-Hop's Bloodstream
episodes.description:
Thirty years ago Peanut Butter Wolf started Stones Throw to release the music of Charizma, his friend killed in 1993. What grew out of that grief became underground music's most important indie label — and the thing flowing through it, from the first Madlib records on, is jazz.
 Madlib's Yesterday's New Quintet played the samples live, Shades of Blue reworked the Blue Note vault, and Dilla's Donuts closed the loop in 2006. Listening pick: Angles Without Edges (2001). Told fast — this is the short one.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #14 The Listening Bar: Jazz's Quietest Boom
episodes.description:
The hottest room in jazz has no stage. The draw is a turntable, serious speakers, a chair facing them, and a house rule from postwar Tokyo's jazz kissa: you do not talk over the record. That ritual is now the template for hi-fi listening bars worldwide — listening became a night out again.
 From Chigusa, founded in 1933, to In Sheep's Clothing and Gold Line in Los Angeles, in the streaming age people pay for the opposite of free and instant: one record, played whole, loud, together. Listening pick: one full side of A Love Supreme on the best system you can find.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #13 Nubya Garcia: London's Horn
episodes.description:
A tight spotlight: Nubya Garcia, the tenor saxophonist carrying London's jazz wave — post-bop in one hand, the Caribbean in the other, with dub, calypso, and club music all native to her sound. A youth programme in Camden produced the horn that explains the last ten years of London jazz.
 Her debut Source landed a Mercury Prize shortlist; Odyssey has her writing for string orchestra. Listening pick: "Pace" from Source (2020). Keep it punchy — this is the short one.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #12 Strange Fruit: The Song They Tried to Bury
episodes.description:
Café Society, 1939: the room goes dark, one spotlight, and Billie Holiday sings "Strange Fruit." It began as evidence — Lawrence Beitler's photograph of the Marion, Indiana lynching — became Abel Meeropol's poem, and then the most dangerous three minutes in American music.
 Her own label would not touch it; tiny Commodore Records recorded it instead, and Holiday paid for the song for the rest of her life. Listening pick: the 1939 Commodore side, then Nina Simone's 1965 version.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #11 Chicago: The Sound of the Great Migration, Still Moving
episodes.description:
Chicago's founding myth is a train schedule. The Illinois Central ran from the Mississippi Delta straight to the South Side, and riding it came hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners — with New Orleans music in their hands. Chicago is where that music first got recorded properly, and where it learned to be modern.
 King Oliver at Lincoln Gardens, Armstrong's Hot Fives in 1925, the AACM building its own institution in 1965, and International Anthem still running the same play a century later. Listening pick: "Cornet Chop Suey" (1926).
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #10 BADBADNOTGOOD: The Bridge Band
episodes.description:
In 2011, three jazz students in Toronto posted a shaky video playing Odd Future songs as a jazz trio — and hip-hop's loudest crew shared it with the world. BADBADNOTGOOD became the bridge band: the group a generation walked across from rap to jazz without noticing the water underneath.
 From backing Ghostface Killah on Sour Soul to co-producing for Kendrick Lamar, then circling back to Talk Memory, their most purely improvised record. Listening pick: "Time Moves Slow" from IV.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #9 Makaya McCraven: The Beat Scientist
episodes.description:
Makaya McCraven records his band live, then takes the tapes home and builds new music out of them — sampling his own players like a hip-hop producer. In the Moment, Universal Beings, and In These Times are the proof: the beat scientist rewired what a jazz drummer does.
 He is the sound of Chicago's International Anthem label in one person. Listening pick: "The Jaunt" from In the Moment, then the title track of In These Times as the deep cut.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #8 Monk: The Night New York Took His License to Play
episodes.description:
In the summer of 1951, Thelonious Monk lost the little police-issued cabaret card every New York musician needed to work a room that served drinks — and with it, six years of playing his own city. He spent the exile composing some of the greatest music in the American canon.
 The Baroness Pannonica took the rap with him, and in 1957 the card came back: the Five Spot comeback, next to a young John Coltrane. Listening pick: Brilliant Corners, then Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #7 Ezra Collective: Jazz for the Dancefloor
episodes.description:
The biggest jazz band in Britain is a dance band. Ezra Collective — five Londoners who met as teenagers in the Tomorrow's Warriors youth programme — won the Mercury Prize in 2023, Group of the Year at the BRITs, and headlined Wembley Arena, with no singer out front and nothing sanded down.
 Listening pick: "Victory Dance" from Where I'm Meant To Be, then the full album Dance, No One's Watching — two horns, keys, bass, and drums built to move a room.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #6 New York: The Capital Holds
episodes.description:
New York nearly lost jazz in the seventies. Instead it rebuilt — and held the capital. From the Village Vanguard, open since February 22, 1935, to the Five Spot and the loft era, this is the infrastructure story: the rooms, the leases, and the stubborn people who kept the music housed.
 Monk's quartet opened at the Five Spot on July 18, 1957 with a young John Coltrane beside him; Frederick P. Rose Hall opened October 18, 2004 as the rebuild's symbol; and Smalls now streams its tiny basement to the world.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #5 Samara Joy: The Voice That Brought the Standards Back
episodes.description:
A kid from Castle Hill in the Bronx, raised on gospel with the Savettes, wins the Sarah Vaughan competition in 2019 — and then runs the table: Best New Artist at the 2023 Grammys and a sixth Grammy for Portrait in February 2026. Samara Joy made the standards feel new again.
 Start with Portrait, cut at Van Gelder Studio — the same room as Coltrane — and hear a singer in her twenties phrase like she has all the time in the world.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #4 A Love Supreme: The Prayer Coltrane Recorded in One Day
episodes.description:
One December day in 1964 — December 9, at Rudy Van Gelder's studio — John Coltrane's quartet recorded a four-part prayer in essentially a single session: A Love Supreme. How it was made, and why this record, of all records, got canonized.
 The four-note "Acknowledgement" motif, the poem hidden in the liner notes and chanted back through the horn, the Smithsonian manuscript, and the Saint John Coltrane Church — plus the 2021 Live in Seattle tapes as the album's afterlife.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #3 The Sweep: Six Cities, One Week in Jazz
episodes.description:
One episode, six cities, one week in jazz. The Sweep checks the pulse in Los Angeles, New York, Chicago, Paris, London, and Tokyo — residencies, festivals, and the rooms where the music is actually moving right now.
 Robert Glasper's eighth Robtober runs at Blue Note New York through November 1, SMOKE hosts its Monk Festival, Paris is mid–Jazz sur Seine (October 9–24), and London is counting down to the EFG London Jazz Festival, November 13–22.
 Love you madly.

episodes.title: #214 David Ellison: Hollywood's New Landlord
episodes.description:
Fifteen years ago David Ellison was the rich kid whose flying movie flopped. On October 6, 2026, he closed the deal that put Warner Bros. and Paramount in the same hands, and no mogul in history has held a combination like it.
 The education in between was real: financing other people's slates, learning the business title by title, and producing Top Gun: Maverick, the movie that made him credible. Then came the Redstone fight for Paramount, Bari Weiss at CBS News, and a hostile run at Warner Bros. Discovery backed by his father's Oracle fortune, with the data centers and cloud empire humming underneath the studio.
 Larry Ellison was the showman. David is the quiet operator running the same…

episodes.title: #213 Larry Ellison: Winning by Buying
episodes.description:
For one day in September 2025, Larry Ellison was the richest man alive. He was 81, and the money did not come from a new invention. It came from forty years of databases, data centers, and a doctrine he never apologized for: if you cannot beat them, buy them.
 Ellison started with a borrowed name and a CIA codename. Oracle was a covert project before it was a company, and the company nearly died in 1990 before the acquisition spree that swallowed PeopleSoft, Sun, and half the enterprise software world. He won the America's Cup from 8-1 down because quitting was not in the operating system. He bought 98 percent of a Hawaiian island. And in his eighties, the AI boom made his infrastructure…

episodes.title: #211 Arturo Schomburg: The Man Who Built the Counter-Archive
episodes.description:
Arturo Schomburg was a kid in San Juan when a teacher told him Black people had no history. He spent the rest of his life proving her wrong, one book at a time.
 This episode follows the Afro-Puerto Rican collector who built the archive Black history runs on, and widens into the bigger question his life poses: who decides what gets saved? Slavery's records were written by enslavers, so Schomburg built a counter-archive inside the public library — and a century later we're still working out what that means.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #210 Mongolia: How to Stay Yourself Between Russia and China
episodes.description:
Mongolia is the emptiest country on Earth — about two people per square kilometer — and a third of it still moves with the seasons. It's also the homeland of the largest land empire in history, now sitting quietly between Russia and China.
 This episode traces how that happens: nomadism as a technology, not a rootlessness; Chinggis Khan and the empire that fragmented into other people's countries; Buddhism, Soviet decades, and a revolution that killed no one; and the modern squeeze of selling nearly everything to one neighbor while buying fuel from the other. How does a small country between two giants stay itself?
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #209 Pompeii: The City That Didn't Know It Was Ending
episodes.description:
In 79 AD, Pompeii was a working Roman city of bakeries, bars, election posters, and graffiti — and almost nobody there knew the mountain behind it was a volcano. Latin didn't even have a word for one. Then, over about eighteen hours, the city stopped mid-sentence.
 This episode tells it as a story: the ordinary day, the warnings nobody could read, Pliny watching from across the bay, the strange fact that most people actually escaped — and how a city gets forgotten for 1,500 years, then dug up to become the most famous disaster in the world. What we lost, what we learned, and why we can't stop looking.
 Follow along for the next deep dive.
 Stay curious.

episodes.title: #208 New Hollywood: The Decade the Directors Took Over
episodes.description:
In 1967, American movies changed their mind about everything. The studio system that had run Hollywood for forty years collapsed — and for one strange decade, the keys went to film-school kids, method actors who looked like people you knew, and cinematographers who shot in the dark. The Godfather, Taxi Driver, Chinatown, Jaws: the most celebrated run of films in the country's history came from the industry briefly losing control of itself.
 This episode traces how it happened: the Paramount Decrees and television gutting the old studios, Bonnie and Clyde and Easy Rider proving a young audience existed, the 1968 ratings system replacing the censors, and the auteurs — Coppola, Scorsese,…

episodes.title: #207 Iran-Contra: The Scandal That Pardoned Itself
episodes.description:
In October 1986, a cargo plane carrying weapons was shot down over Nicaragua, and the sole survivor started talking. Within two months, the Reagan White House was admitting to one of the strangest schemes in American history: selling missiles to Iran — the enemy — and secretly funneling the profits to a rebel army Congress had explicitly cut off. And that was only the half of it that got hearings.
 This episode walks the whole machine: the Boland Amendments, Oliver North and the Enterprise's Swiss accounts, the televised hearings, the Walsh investigation, and the Christmas Eve pardons that ended accountability. Then the darker thread — what the CIA's own inspector general conceded in 1998…

episodes.title: #206 The Ten Percent: CAA, WME, and the Invention of the Agent
episodes.description:
Behind almost every famous name in entertainment stands someone you've never heard of — and they take ten percent of everything. The agent might be the most powerful job in Hollywood that nobody outside it understands, and it wasn't designed. It was improvised, piece by piece, by people solving very specific problems.
 This episode traces that invention: vaudeville-era exploitation and how the 10% commission became the norm, William Morris and MCA setting the template, Lew Wasserman's Winchester '73 deal that rewired star pay, and the night in 1975 when five young agents quit William Morris and founded CAA. We get into the deals and the structure — packaging, the fees studios paid agencies…

episodes.title: #205 1920s Harlem: How to Spot a Renaissance
episodes.description:
In the 1920s, a few square miles of Manhattan became the capital of Black culture — and for a moment, the center of American art itself. Hughes, Hurston, Ellington, Aaron Douglas: an entire generation arrived at once, in one neighborhood. But the Harlem Renaissance wasn't an accident. It had ingredients.
 This episode takes Harlem apart: the Great Migration and the real-estate accident that made Harlem Black, the institutions that organized it — The Crisis, Opportunity, the Civic Club dinner, Alain Locke's The New Negro — the Cotton Club paradox of Black genius performing for whites-only audiences, and jazz as the distribution network that carried Harlem everywhere. Then the end: the…

episodes.title: #17 Por Que São Paulo Parece Mais Branca? Raça, Imigração e a Geografia do Brasil (Português)
episodes.description:
São Paulo não se tornou uma das grandes cidades mais brancas das Américas por acaso. Foi política de Estado. Depois da abolição, em 1888, as elites brasileiras perseguiram o branqueamento — subsidiando a imigração europeia em escala massiva para diluir a população negra do país — e São Paulo foi a sala de máquinas desse projeto.
 Este episódio acompanha como essa máquina funcionou: mais de um milhão de europeus chegando entre 1890 e 1914, o mercado de trabalho em dois níveis que levou os imigrantes para as fábricas e o comércio enquanto os afro-brasileiros eram empurrados para as margens, e a transformação demográfica que se seguiu — a autodeclaração de pretos caindo de 19,2% em 1872 para…

episodes.title: #17 Why Does São Paulo Look Whiter? Race, Immigration and the Geography of Brazil (English)
episodes.description:
São Paulo didn't end up one of the whitest big cities in the Americas by accident. It was policy. After abolition in 1888, Brazil's elites pursued branqueamento — whitening — subsidizing European immigration on a massive scale to dilute the country's Black population, and São Paulo was the machine's engine room.
 This episode traces how that machine worked: more than a million Europeans arriving between 1890 and 1914, the two-tier labor market that moved immigrants into factories and commerce while Afro-Brazilians were pushed to the margins, and the demographic reshaping that followed — Black self-identification falling from 19.2% in 1872 to under 5% by 1990. We map the geography it built:…

episodes.title: #204 Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: The Film That Watched Itself
episodes.description:
In 1968, filmmaker William Greaves took a cast and crew into Central Park to shoot a screen test — and quietly designed the production so his crew would rebel against him on camera. The result, Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One, is a film inside a film inside a film: actors performing a melodrama, a director performing incompetence, and a mostly-white crew secretly filming their own mutiny while a Black director watched it all unfold exactly as he'd predicted in his notebooks.
 This episode unpacks the word behind it — symbiotaxiplasm, life arranging itself into shared reality, and the "psycho" Greaves added for the paranoia and ego that surface the moment people know they're being watched —…

episodes.title: #203 Local Natives and the Last Indie Band of the 2000s
episodes.description:
Local Natives were five kids from Orange County who moved into a Silver Lake house together, named their debut album after it — Gorilla Manor — and became one of the defining bands of the 2000s indie era. This episode tells their story as the door into that whole world: the blogs that could make a band overnight, Pitchfork as kingmaker, Spaceland and the Echo, and a sound built on stacked harmonies and restless percussion.
 Then the era turns: Hummingbird, made with Aaron Dessner in the shadow of grief; streaming playlists replacing the blogs; Silver Lake pricing out its own scene; and the band's long arc through lineup changes to where they stand today — and what the indie era permanently…

episodes.title: #202 The Polygraph: The Machine That Never Detected a Lie
episodes.description:
For a hundred years, the polygraph has decided who gets hired, who gets believed, and who goes to prison — without ever actually detecting a lie. This episode traces the machine from John Larson's 1921 Berkeley prototype and the inventor who lived to regret it, through Marston (who also created Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth), the CIA and NSA screening empires, and the math problem that breaks the whole idea: screen ten thousand people to find ten spies, and you flag a thousand innocents.
 Plus the human cost in both directions — Jeffrey Deskovic, who failed a polygraph, falsely confessed, and lost sixteen years; Aldrich Ames, who passed twice while selling secrets — and the twist at the…

episodes.title: #201 Smoke Shops & Dispensaries: The Business Behind the Counter
episodes.description:
There are roughly 18,000 smoke shops in America, and almost nobody understands how they make money. This episode goes behind the counter: startup costs from $50,000 to $180,000, the margin ladder that runs the whole business — cigarettes at 4 to 6 percent just to pull traffic, glass and hemp at 50 to 70 percent paying the rent — plus the distributors, the 800-store chains, and the high-risk payment processing that can freeze a shop's money overnight.
 Then the legal patchwork they sell under — the federal paraphernalia law, FDA vape crackdowns, New York's Operation Padlock — and the big question at the center: are these shops quietly building the storefronts, zoning positions, and customer…

episodes.title: #200 The Curiosity Continues...
episodes.description:
Two hundred episodes, five months, and more rabbit holes than I ever expected. We're back for another human check-in, and this time I'm reflecting on just how far The Eclectic Polymath has come, what I've learned along the way, and how this little experiment in curiosity keeps evolving.
 I revisit some of my favorite episodes from the last stretch, the random moments that inspired them, and the connections that have started to emerge across everything we've explored. From Bruce Lee and Big Ben to Erykah Badu, Marvel, marriage, and everything in between, I'm learning more about what makes a great episode, what sparks my curiosity, and how this podcast has become my own personal curriculum.
…

episodes.title: #006 Trying to Run My Life With Meta's Muse AI Agent
episodes.description:
AI agents have been talked about as the future for a while now. But what happens when you actually give one access to your apps, your calendar, and the projects you're working on?
In Episode 6 of Approachable AI, Joshua returns to explore Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, and puts it to work on everything from turning hundreds of saved Instagram posts into a personalized Google Map to helping automate his other podcast, The Eclectic Polymath. He also experiments with using AI to track personal goals, manage his schedule, discover new places, and take some of the busywork out of everyday life.
Along the way, there are plenty of unexpected discoveries, technical hiccups, and ideas that…

episodes.title: #199 The Chakras: Blocked and Unblocked
episodes.description: What does it actually look like — in a real person's body, mind, and daily life — when an energy center is blocked, and what does it look like when it opens? This is the full chakra map: all seven centers, from root to crown, with the traditional Sanskrit wisdom, the specific bodily and mental indicators of blockage, concrete modern case studies of each one blocked and unblocked, and the practices that open them — both the ancient (specific asanas, pranayama, bija mantras) and the modern (somatic therapy, breathwork, HRV biofeedback). We trace where the system really comes from — medieval Tantra's Sat-Cakra-Nirupana, not the Vedas — and how the rainbow chart got its colors from 20th-century…

episodes.title: #198 Seinfeld: Who Was Really the Brains?
episodes.description: Everyone says Larry David was the real brains behind Seinfeld — but what actually went down? This is the full rundown: two stand-up comics, one fateful 1988 meeting with NBC's Rick Ludwin, and a pilot that tested so badly the network research memo got hung on the writers' room wall. We reconstruct the creative ledger — Larry wrote 62 of the first 126 episodes and gave the show its misanthropic voice, Jerry supplied the premise, the performance, and the quality control — then follow the money: $3.1 billion in syndication, Jerry's billion-dollar net worth, Larry's hundreds of millions, the famous $100M+ season-10 offer Jerry walked away from, and the $500M Netflix deal. We cover Larry's…

episodes.title: #197 Spirit Halloween: The Business of the Pop-Up
episodes.description: Every fall, Spirit Halloween appears out of nowhere — 1,500 stores in dead malls and empty big boxes across America — and then vanishes by mid-November. How does a store that exists for 60 days make money? This is the full anatomy of the machine: the ~$1 billion seasonal business, the real-estate arbitrage of vacant retail space (one real lease: $30,000 flat for three and a half months), the buildout crews that convert an empty box into a Halloween superstore in days, the 52,000 seasonal workers, the teardown on November 1st where unsold inventory gets stored instead of liquidated, and the unit economics — roughly $100–150K profit per store in two months. We trace Spirit from Joe Marver's…

episodes.title: #196 Charlie Sheen: The Truth Behind "Winning"
episodes.description: In 2011, Charlie Sheen — the highest-paid actor on television — went on live TV and declared he had "tiger blood" and "Adonis DNA," that he was "winning." America laughed, then watched it curdle in real time. But what was actually going on? This is the full story: the Malibu kid who became a movie star in Platoon and Wall Street, the $1.8 million-an-episode king of Two and a Half Men, and the unraveling — the rehabs, the Plaza Hotel, the firing, the $100 million lawsuit, the disastrous Detroit tour, and the media machine that turned a man's breakdown into content. We separate the documented facts from the lore, trace the money from peak to collapse, and follow Sheen through the 2015 HIV…

episodes.title: #195 Ari Emanuel: The Agent Who Ate Hollywood
episodes.description: He started as a kid from Chicago with dyslexia, ADHD, and a phone he wouldn't put down. Then Ari Emanuel got fired from his own job — and built Endeavor out of a walkout, turned a talent agency into a private-equity empire, and bought the UFC and the WWE along the way. This is the full story: the ICM walkout, the Silver Lake deal, the $2.4 billion IMG bet, the $4 billion UFC gamble, the $21.4 billion TKO combination, and the negotiation playbook — information, persistence, leverage — that made him the most feared man in Hollywood. We trace the three-act history of power from Wasserman to Ovitz to Emanuel, dissect the WGA war over packaging, separate the verified stories from the Hollywood…

episodes.title: #194 Obama's Shadow Wars: Drones, Raids, and the Power Vacuums They Left Behind
episodes.description:
Three days after Barack Obama became president, missiles struck Pakistan. It was the beginning of a new kind of American war — no invasions, no occupations. Instead: drones, a kill list, and small teams of operators. 563 strikes across Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia, compared to 57 under Bush.
 This episode goes inside the machine: the "light footprint" doctrine, the disposition matrix, the "Terror Tuesday" targeting meetings, personality strikes versus signature strikes — and the two institutions that ran the overlapping wars, the CIA and JSOC. A bureaucracy for deciding who lives and who dies, built in secret.
 Then the raids: the one that worked — Abbottabad, May 2011, Bin Laden dead in…

episodes.title: #193 Why Cuba Is Where People Go to Vanish
episodes.description:
"Fake my death, go to Cuba, that's the only option." Kendrick Lamar compressed an entire American fantasy into one line on "ELEMENT." (DAMN., 2017). He didn't do it — but the line works because every American ear already knows what Cuba means: the place you go when you need to disappear.
 Underneath the lyric is real history. Assata Shakur escaped prison in 1979 and received political asylum in Cuba, living there beyond America's reach for over four decades. She wasn't the first — the 1960s and '70s saw "take me to Cuba" become the signature demand of airline hijackers, while figures like Robert F. Williams and Huey Newton also fled to the island.
 Here's the twist the research uncovered:…

episodes.title: #192 Marriage: The Business Behind "I Do"
episodes.description:
Two people can love each other for years without the government caring very much. Then they say "I do," sign a document, and suddenly courts, tax authorities, insurers, employers, immigration officials, and inheritance law all have something to say about their relationship. So what actually happens when love becomes marriage?
 This episode traces marriage from an institution built around kinship, property, inheritance, and family alliances into the modern love story—and follows the wedding industry that grew around it. We get into diamond rings, white dresses, registries, bachelor parties, the so-called "wedding tax," destination weddings, and why a celebration that can legally happen at a…

episodes.title: #191 Diamonds: Love, Scarcity, and the Most Engineered Symbol in Romance
episodes.description:
A diamond is carbon arranged in an extraordinary way. So how did a tiny crystal formed deep beneath the Earth become one of the most recognizable and expensive symbols of love in the world?
 This episode follows the diamond from mine to engagement ring: how natural diamonds form, how rough stones are cut and graded, what the 4Cs actually tell you, why cut often matters more than the specifications people obsess over, and how natural, lab-grown, moissanite, and other alternatives really differ. We also get into the modern buying game—magic carat thresholds, grading reports, jewelry markups, insurance, resale, and why a ring's appraisal value can be very different from what anyone would…

episodes.title: #16 Rua Oscar Freire: Como São Paulo Construiu Sua Própria Rodeo Drive (Português)
episodes.description: Distritos de luxo não surgem por acaso. Eles são construídos aos poucos — por meio da geografia, da arquitetura, do dinheiro, do gosto e da decisão coletiva de que um determinado endereço vale mais do que as ruas ao seu redor.Este episódio acompanha como a Rua Oscar Freire evoluiu de uma tranquila rua residencial no bairro dos Jardins, em São Paulo, para se tornar um dos corredores de compras de luxo mais conhecidos do mundo. Passamos pelas raízes urbanísticas de cidade-jardim da região, pela chegada de artistas e designers, pela ascensão de nomes da moda brasileira e, mais tarde, pela concentração de marcas internacionais como Louis Vuitton, Dior e Cartier. Também exploramos a reforma de…

episodes.title: #16 Rua Oscar Freire: How São Paulo Built Its Rodeo Drive (English)
episodes.description: Luxury districts don’t appear by accident. They’re built slowly — through geography, architecture, money, taste, and the collective decision that one particular address means more than the streets around it.This episode traces how Rua Oscar Freire evolved from a quiet residential street in São Paulo’s Jardins district into one of the world’s best-known luxury shopping corridors. We follow the neighborhood’s garden-city roots, the arrival of artists and designers, the rise of Brazilian fashion names, and the later concentration of international brands like Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Cartier. We also look at the 2006–2007 renovation that buried utility lines and widened sidewalks, helping turn…

episodes.title: #190 Church Hierarchy: From Apostles and Bishops to Pastors and Popes
episodes.description:
Jesus didn't leave behind an org chart. There were no dioceses, seminaries, annual conferences, denominational boards, or Vatican departments. Yet Christianity eventually built one of the most elaborate collections of institutions in human history.
 This episode traces how that happened—from the original meaning of apostle and the rise of bishops, priests, elders, pastors, and deacons to the radically different systems those titles belong to today. We move through Catholic apostolic succession and the Vatican, Orthodox bishops without a universal pope, the organizational explosion of the Protestant Reformation, and the difference between being called, ordained, elected, appointed, or simply…

episodes.title: #15 A Máquina de Imigração do Brasil: Como o País se Tornou Tão Misturado (Português)
episodes.description: O Brasil não se tornou uma das sociedades mais miscigenadas do mundo simplesmente por acaso. Durante décadas, o governo recrutou ativamente pessoas de várias partes do mundo — pagando passagens, encaminhando recém-chegados por uma enorme infraestrutura de imigração e enviando famílias para uma economia que estava sendo reconstruída após a escravidão.Este episódio acompanha esse sistema a partir da Hospedaria dos Imigrantes, em São Paulo, por onde passaram cerca de 2,5 milhões de pessoas, e da enorme imigração italiana que forneceu mão de obra às fazendas de café depois da abolição. Seguimos alemães, portugueses, espanhóis, imigrantes do Leste Europeu e, mais tarde, os japoneses — desde a…

episodes.title: #15 Brazil's Immigration Machine: How the Country Became So Mixed (English)
episodes.description: Brazil didn't simply become one of the world's most mixed societies by accident. For decades, the government actively recruited people from across the world—paying for passages, funneling newcomers through massive immigration infrastructure, and sending families into an economy being rebuilt after slavery.This episode traces that system from São Paulo's Hospedaria dos Imigrantes, which processed roughly 2.5 million arrivals, through the enormous Italian migration that supplied coffee plantations with labor after abolition. We follow Germans, Portuguese, Spaniards, Eastern Europeans, and eventually the Japanese—from the Kasato Maru arriving in Santos in 1908 to Brazil becoming home to the…

episodes.title: #189 DC's Identity Crisis: How the Original Superhero Empire Lost Hollywood to Marvel
episodes.description:
Superman invented the superhero. Batman became one of the most adaptable fictional characters ever created. Wonder Woman became a global icon. So how did DC — the company that built the foundation of superhero culture — lose Hollywood's center of gravity to Marvel?
 This episode traces DC's extraordinary history, from the birth of Superman and the rise of Batman through Superman: The Movie, Batman, the DC Animated Universe, Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy, the DCEU experiment, and the current James Gunn era. Along the way, we explore why DC repeatedly produced incredible individual stories while struggling to create the kind of interconnected cinematic system that transformed Marvel…

episodes.title: #188 Marvel's Dark Years: How the MCU Lost Its Magic
episodes.description:
For more than a decade, Marvel Studios seemed unstoppable. What began as an ambitious experiment in interconnected storytelling became Hollywood's most successful franchise, culminating in Avengers: Endgame. Then something changed. The movies kept coming, the universe kept expanding, but the magic became harder to sustain.
 This episode traces Marvel's rise under Kevin Feige, the creative decisions that made its early success possible, and the pressures that followed. We explore Disney's streaming ambitions, the explosion of Disney+ series, production challenges, and why genuinely inventive projects like WandaVision could coexist with increasingly inconsistent films and television.
 But…

episodes.title: #14 Quilombos: Black Resistance, Sovereignty, and Freedom in Brazil (Português)
episodes.description: A escravidão no Brasil não passou sem resistência.
